# Who is the second loop? Measuring how often a person has to step in to keep an AI system ultrastable

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that an AI system that runs itself only needs good monitoring; when something breaks, a probe catches it and a fix follows. This paper argues otherwise: monitoring fixes instances. Staying viable for a year also needs a loop that changes the rules, thresholds and work specs when the same trouble keeps coming back, and that loop has to be judged on whether its changes work.

Ashby's ultrastable system has two loops. The fast one fixes ordinary trouble. The slow one changes the system itself when the fast one can't. We asked who plays the slow loop here, and counted.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 5 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

For two weeks the owner kept typing the same kind of message: the changelog is quiet, pull requests are stale, papers never got posted. Each one was a person doing the slow loop's job. This paper turns that into numbers: how often a person stepped in, whether the system's own slow-loop changes ever worked, whether its work items could be misread, and whether its own papers are true in its code. [2]

This matters now because the usual answer, monitoring plus fixes is enough to run unattended, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. A person acting as the slow loop. Every owner message that redirects the system is a slow-loop action done by hand. We count distinct owner-driven sessions that changed the repository in a week; the target is none. [2]
2. A slow loop that never learns. Before this change the slow loop had judged 91 of its own steps and reverted all 91. A loop that only moves is not adapting. Its keep rate is now an essential variable, and its first step on that variable is to change its own settle window. [2]
3. Work an agent can misread. A vague item gets a plausible wrong fix. An item passes intake only with a machine-checkable done check, the metric it should move, an out-of-scope line and a live proof step. [2]
4. Papers the code does not live up to. Each finding in each paper names its mechanism and the measurement that tests it. The share that meets its target is an essential variable, so a paper that drifts from the code pushes the slow loop to build, not to edit the paper. [2]
5. Limits on everything that matters. Every essential variable, including the four added here, has limits, so the slow loop can fire on each. [2]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [2]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. A person acting as the slow loop: owner_interventions reads the provenance ledger every tick as an essential variable with a ladder (SECOND-LOOP-2, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
2. A slow loop that never learns: keep_rate reads the loop's own verdicts; the ladder edits settle_ticks and patience_ticks in doctrine/ultrastability.json (SECOND-LOOP-2, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
3. Work an agent can misread: fails any new open item missing one of the four parts; a shrink-only baseline holds the old ones (SPEC-GATE-1, `foundation/specgate.py`)
4. Papers the code does not live up to: research_findings_met_share measures every finding of every paper (RESEARCH-LOOP-1, `foundation/research.py`); research_in_code holds the share at 1.0 with a build ladder (RESEARCH-LOOP-1, `doctrine/ultrastability.json`)
5. Limits on everything that matters: the check fails a variable with no limits (ASHBY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. A person acting as the slow loop. Put in place: owner_interventions reads the provenance ledger every tick as an essential variable with a ladder. Check it with one number, owner-driven thread sessions that changed the repository in the last 7 days (ops/provenance.jsonl), and set a limit for it (<= 0 is the limit we use).
2. A slow loop that never learns. Put in place: keep_rate reads the loop's own verdicts; the ladder edits settle_ticks and patience_ticks in doctrine/ultrastability.json. Check it with one number, share of second-order steps that brought the variable back inside its limits and were kept, and set a limit for it (>= 0.25 is the limit we use).
3. Work an agent can misread. Put in place: fails any new open item missing one of the four parts; a shrink-only baseline holds the old ones. Check it with one number, share of open work items with a done check, a prediction, an out-of-scope line and a live proof (foundation/specgate.py), and set a limit for it (>= 0.9 is the limit we use).
4. Papers the code does not live up to. Put in place: research_findings_met_share measures every finding of every paper. Check it with one number, share of every finding in every paper whose own measurement meets its target, excluding this metric (RESEARCH-LOOP-1), and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
5. Limits on everything that matters. Put in place: the check fails a variable with no limits. Check it with one number, share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json), and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 1 of 5 of these checks pass today. Owner-driven thread sessions that changed the repository in the last 7 days (ops/provenance.jsonl) reads 52 (n = None; source: ops/provenance.jsonl, last 7 days). Share of second-order steps that brought the variable back inside its limits and were kept reads 0.0 (n = 91; source: ops/ultrastability.jsonl verdicts). Share of open work items with a done check, a prediction, an out-of-scope line and a live proof (foundation/specgate.py) reads 0.291 (n = None; source: foundation/specgate.py over docs/issues). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.
